The house received the morning as if it had been expecting an apology from it. Helena moved through the corridor with a careful hand upon the banister, and even that quiet pressure seemed to wake a memory in the wood. Every room had a habit of keeping yesterday in some visible corner. A ribbon lay where no ribbon ought to be; a glove had the air of a remark postponed rather than forgotten. She paused before the breakfast table and studied the silver as if polish itself might restore an earlier agreement. The servants spoke softly, not from fear, but because the household had fallen into a way of treating feeling as if it were breakable china. When the clock in the small drawing room struck nine, its note seemed less to divide the hour than to accuse it. Helena sat, unfolded a letter she already knew by heart, and discovered that the lines had not altered, though her patience with them had. Outside, the garden made a composed show of order, yet every bed of flowers leaned a little too far toward neglect.
